items.prompt: Which word is formed by blending the sounds /p/ /ĭ/ /g/?
items.rationale: Pushing the three sounds /p/, /ĭ/, and /g/ together forms the word “pig.”

items.prompt: In which order should a learner blend the sounds in the word “top”?
items.rationale: The word “top” begins with /t/, has /ŏ/ in the middle, and ends with /p/.

items.prompt: Which action shows a learner correctly blending /h/ /ă/ /t/?
choices: Pushes the sounds together and says “hat”
Says each sound as a separate word
items.answer: Pushes the sounds together and says “hat”
items.rationale: Blending means pushing the individual sounds together to read the whole word “hat.”

items.prompt: What happens when the sounds /p/ /ĭ/ /g/ are blended?
choices: They stay as three separate words.
items.rationale: Blending joins the individual sounds in order so the learner can read the whole word “pig.”

items.prompt: Which word is made by blending the letter sounds /k/ /ă/ /t/?
items.rationale: Blending /k/ /ă/ /t/ gives c-a-t, so “cat” is the correct word.

items.prompt: Which word has the short i sound?
items.rationale: The i in “sit” makes the short /ĭ/ sound; the other choices have short a.

items.prompt: Which word starts with /m/ and ends with /p/?
items.rationale: “Map” starts with /m/ and ends with /p/, with short a in the middle.

items.prompt: Which word uses the short a sound in the middle?
items.rationale: The middle vowel in “bat” is short a; the middle vowels in the other choices are short i.

items.prompt: Which word has a short u sound?
items.rationale: Cut is sounded out as /k/ /u/ /t/, with a short u sound.

items.prompt: Which word is made by blending the sounds /m/, /o/, and /p/?
items.rationale: Blending /m/, /o/, and /p/ makes the word mop.

items.prompt: In which word does the middle letter make a short e sound?
items.rationale: Hen is sounded out as /h/ /e/ /n/, with a short e sound.

items.prompt: A word starts with /m/ and ends with /p/. Which spelling has a short o sound in the middle?
items.rationale: Mop is sounded out as /m/ /o/ /p/, with a short o sound.

items.prompt: Which word ends with “-ng”?
items.rationale: “Ring” ends with “-ng,” which makes one sound.

items.prompt: Which word ends with “-nk”?
items.rationale: “Bank” ends with the joined letters “-nk,” which make one sound.

items.prompt: Which word is formed by adding “-ng” to “ri”?
items.rationale: Adding “-ng” to “ri” forms “ring.”

items.prompt: Which choice is the sight word that starts with s and ends with d?
items.rationale: “Said” is a Set 4 sight word, and it starts with s and ends with d.

items.prompt: Which choice is the three-letter sight word that starts with w?
items.rationale: “Was” is a Set 4 sight word with three letters, and it starts with w.

items.prompt: Which choice is the sight word with the letter r in the middle?
items.rationale: “Are” is a Set 4 sight word, and r is its middle letter.

items.prompt: Which choice is the sight word that starts with th and ends with y?
items.rationale: “They” is a Set 4 sight word, and it starts with th and ends with y.

items.prompt: The sentence reads, “The cat is asleep.” Which voice should you use when reading it?
items.rationale: A period shows that a statement is complete. A calm, flat voice fits this sentence.

items.prompt: Which punctuation mark should end the sentence: “Do you like apples”
items.rationale: The sentence asks a question, so it needs a question mark to show a rising, questioning voice.

items.prompt: The sentence reads, “Can you help me?” Which voice should you use when reading it?
items.rationale: A question mark signals that the sentence is asking something, so the voice should rise with curiosity.

items.prompt: Which punctuation mark should end an announcement that should be read with excitement: “The show has started”
items.rationale: An exclamation mark shows strong excitement and helps the announcement sound lively and enthusiastic.

items.prompt: Choose the sight word that asks for the name of something.
items.rationale: “What” is the sight word used to ask for the name or identity of something.

items.prompt: Choose the sight word that asks about a place.
items.rationale: “Where” is the sight word used to ask about a place or location.

items.prompt: Choose the sight word that means to direct your eyes toward something.
items.rationale: “Look” is the sight word used to direct one’s eyes toward something.

items.prompt: Choose the sight word used when inviting someone to move closer.
items.rationale: “Come” is the sight word used to invite someone to move closer.

items.prompt: Which word begins with two consonant sounds?
items.rationale: The word “frog” begins with the consonant blend “fr,” so its first two letters make two consonant sounds.

items.prompt: Which word ends with two consonant sounds?
items.rationale: The word “lamp” ends with the consonant blend “mp,” so its last two letters make two consonant sounds.

items.prompt: Which letters make the blend at the beginning of “stop”?
items.rationale: The beginning of “stop” has the consonant blend “st.”

items.prompt: Which letters make the blend at the end of “lamp”?
items.rationale: The ending of “lamp” has the consonant blend “mp.”

items.prompt: A story line says, “The cat sat on the mat.” How should you read it aloud?
choices: Read every word by itself, with a short pause after each word.
Read the words in order with a smooth, natural phrase.
Read only the story’s character and action words.
Read the words from right to left, one word at a time.
items.answer: Read the words in order with a smooth, natural phrase.
items.rationale: Reading the words in order with a smooth, natural phrase shows accurate, fluent reading.

items.prompt: A story line says, “The sun is up. The dog wakes.” How should you read it aloud?
choices: Read the first sentence, pause, then read the second sentence.
Pause after every word in both sentences.
Read the second sentence first, then read the first sentence.
Read both sentences in one long, unbreakable phrase.
items.answer: Read the first sentence, pause, then read the second sentence.
items.rationale: A brief pause at the end of the first sentence helps the reader continue smoothly and accurately.

items.prompt: While reading aloud, you say “mop” instead of “map.” What is the best way to keep your reading accurate?
choices: Keep going and hope the mistake does not change the story.
Go back, say “map,” and then continue reading the sentence.
Change the story so that “mop” makes sense.
Skip the rest of the sentence and begin the next one.
items.answer: Go back, say “map,” and then continue reading the sentence.
items.rationale: Going back, correcting the word, and continuing keeps the reading accurate without stopping the story for long.

items.prompt: A story line says, “I can hop,” said Nan. How should you read this line aloud?
choices: Read the dialogue in a natural voice, pause, then read “said Nan.”
Read the dialogue in a whisper, pause, then read “said Nan.”
Read “said Nan” first, pause, then read the dialogue.
Read the whole line in one voice without a small pause.
items.answer: Read the dialogue in a natural voice, pause, then read “said Nan.”
items.rationale: Reading the dialogue naturally and pausing before the speaker’s words gives the line accurate, smooth phrasing.

items.prompt: Which word starts with the sh sound?
items.rationale: In “ship,” the letters s and h work together to make the /sh/ sound.

items.prompt: Which word ends with the th sound?
items.rationale: In “bath,” the letters t and h work together to make one /th/ sound at the end of the word.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the wh sound?
items.rationale: In “whale,” the letters w and h work together to make the /w/ sound at the beginning of the word.

items.prompt: Mia had a red block. Her brother Jon gave it to her. Who gave Mia the block?
items.rationale: The text says that Jon gave Mia the block.

items.prompt: Nora looked for her shoes. She found them under her bed. Where were the shoes?
items.rationale: The text says that Nora found her shoes under her bed.

items.prompt: Ana baked cookies for lunch. She placed them on a plate. Who baked the cookies?
items.rationale: The text says that Ana baked the cookies.

items.prompt: Jamal is playing basketball with his friends. When the ball rolls away, Jamal runs after it and gets it back. Who is the story about?
items.rationale: Jamal is the main character because the story focuses on his actions during the game.

items.prompt: Anna visits a place where a librarian helps her find a book. She and Dad sit quietly and read together. Where does the story take place?
items.rationale: The librarian, books, and quiet reading show that Anna and Dad are in the library.

items.prompt: Nia put on her shoes and took a ball. At the park, she played on the swings. Which choice tells who the story is about and where it takes place?
items.rationale: Nia is the main character, and the story takes place at the park.

items.prompt: Read one sentence: “Milo put the cup on the table for the cat.” Who put the cup on the table?
items.rationale: Milo is the subject of the sentence and is the one putting the cup on the table.

items.prompt: Ana put a bean in the soil. A plant grew, and a yellow flower opened. Which event belongs at the beginning?
items.rationale: Planting the bean happens first, before the plant grows and the flower opens.

items.prompt: Bo woke up, ate breakfast, brushed his teeth, put on his coat, and left for school. When did Bo brush his teeth?
choices: After Bo put on his coat.
items.rationale: Brushing his teeth comes after breakfast but before putting on his coat, so it is in the middle.

items.prompt: Kim saw a dark cloud, rain began, and then sunshine spread across the sky. Which event belongs at the end of the story?
items.rationale: The sun appearing comes after the cloud arrives and the rain begins, so it is the ending.

items.prompt: Which word is read with a long a sound?
items.rationale: The silent e makes the a in cake say its long sound, /ā/.

items.prompt: Which word has a long i sound?
items.rationale: The silent e makes the i in bike say its long sound, /ī/.

items.prompt: Which word ends with a silent e and has a long o sound?
items.rationale: The final e in note is silent, and the o is read with its long sound, /ō/.

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a word that does not make sense?
choices: The cat ran across the floor and drank a book.
The dog ran across the floor and drank milk.
The bird flew over the tree and ate worms.
The girl jumped over the chair and drank water.
items.answer: The cat ran across the floor and drank a book.
items.rationale: A cat cannot drink a book, so this sentence contains a word that does not make sense.

items.prompt: Which sentence fixes the mistake in “The fish climbed a tree and ate a worm”?
choices: The fish swam in a pond and ate a worm.
The fish climbed a pond and ate a worm.
The fish swam in a tree and ate a worm.
The fish flew in a pond and ate a worm.
items.answer: The fish swam in a pond and ate a worm.
items.rationale: A fish can swim in a pond, so this sentence fixes the words that did not make sense.

items.prompt: I notice that “The bird used a shovel to eat a worm” does not make sense. What should I do next?
choices: Reread it and replace the word.
Skip it and turn to another page.
Change bird to dog and keep going.
Read it again without changing it.
items.answer: Reread it and replace the word.
items.rationale: Rereading the sentence and replacing the wrong word with one that fits fixes the mistake.

items.prompt: Which word completes the sentence: “I ___ to play outside.”
items.rationale: “I want to play outside” is complete because “want” expresses what the speaker wishes to do.

items.prompt: Which word means “a number of things, but not all”?
items.rationale: “Some” means an amount of things that is not the whole amount.

items.prompt: Which word is used to report someone’s words?
items.rationale: “Said” is used to show that someone spoke, as in “Ana said hello.”

items.prompt: Which word means “at or in that place,” not “in this place”?
items.rationale: “There” means at or in that place, while “here” means in this place.

items.prompt: Which word has a long a sound?
items.rationale: In “made,” the a says its long sound, /ā/, as in the word “day.”

items.prompt: Which word has a short u sound?
items.rationale: In “jump,” the u says its short sound, /ŭ/, rather than its long sound, /ū/.

items.prompt: In the word “kit,” which type of vowel sound does the i make?
items.rationale: The i in “kit” says its short sound, /ĭ/, so it is a short vowel sound.

items.prompt: Which word has a long o sound?
items.rationale: In “note,” the o says its long sound, /ō/, while the o in the other words is short.

items.prompt: Mia ___ the puppy every day.
items.rationale: “Feeds” means gives food regularly. The -s ending helps show that Mia does this action.

items.prompt: There are three ___ on the table.
items.rationale: “Dishes” means more than one dish. The -es ending is added to dish when the word ends in sh.

items.prompt: Yesterday, we ___ to the park.
items.rationale: “Walked” describes an action that happened in the past. The -ed ending shows that the walking was yesterday.

items.prompt: Who is speaking in the sentence “I climbed the big tree”?
items.rationale: The word “I” refers to the character who climbed the tree and is speaking.

items.prompt: Which sentence has a character telling the story?
choices: The girl found a shiny leaf.
items.rationale: The pronoun “I” shows that a character inside the story is telling it.

items.prompt: In “Mia lost her ball. She looked for it,” who is telling the story?
items.rationale: The narrator describes Mia in the third person, so someone outside the story is telling it.

items.prompt: In “I helped my mother,” what does the word “I” show?
choices: It shows the speaker's point of view.
It gives the speaker's full name.
It shows an outside narrator's viewpoint.
items.answer: It shows the speaker's point of view.
items.rationale: The word “I” identifies the character who is speaking and shows that the story is told from that character's point of view.

items.prompt: Which word can be split into two smaller words that both make sense?
items.rationale: “Sunset” splits into “sun” and “set,” which are both smaller words.

items.prompt: A child wants to read a word naming a small cake served in a cup. Which split works?
items.rationale: The two smaller words are “cup” and “cake.” Together, they make “cupcake.”

items.prompt: Which split shows the two words in “bookcase”?
items.rationale: “Bookcase” splits into the smaller words “book” and “case.”

items.prompt: What does the contraction “can’t” stand for?
items.rationale: “Can’t” combines “can” and “not,” so it means “can not.”

items.prompt: Which contraction belongs in the sentence: “_____ raining outside today”?
items.rationale: “It’s” stands for “it is,” so the sentence means that it is raining outside today.

items.prompt: In the sentence “I’m ready to read,” which two words does the contraction mean?
items.rationale: “I’m” combines “I” and “am,” so it means “I am.”

items.prompt: Nia jumped out of her seat and shouted, “Yes! Let’s play right now!” What feeling does Nia most likely have?
items.rationale: Nia’s jump, shout, and eager words show that she feels excited.

items.prompt: After the test, Kim pointed to the paper and said, “I got every one right!” Kim most likely feels
items.rationale: Kim’s words show that he feels proud of getting every answer right.

items.prompt: When her cousin arrived, Tara ran to him, hugged him, and said, “I missed you!” Tara most likely feels
items.rationale: Tara’s hug and words show that she feels happy to see her cousin again.

items.prompt: A ball rolled toward Jo. Jo stepped back, held his hands close to his chest, and said, “Please don’t throw it!” Jo most likely feels
items.rationale: Jo’s steps backward, tight hands, and request show that he feels scared.

items.prompt: Which word has the long a sound?
items.rationale: In “rain,” the vowel team ai makes the a sound long.

items.prompt: Which word uses ee to spell the long e sound?
items.rationale: In “feet,” the vowel team ee makes the e sound long.

items.prompt: Which word has the long o sound?
items.rationale: In “boat,” the vowel team oa represents the long o sound, as in “coat.”

items.prompt: Which word rhymes with “feet”?
items.rationale: “Beat” and “feet” have the same long e sound and rhyme. The ea in “beat” represents the long e sound.

items.prompt: Which word is made from the sounds /f/, /l/, and long /ī/?
items.rationale: The sounds /f-l-ī/ spell “fly,” where y sounds like long i.

items.prompt: Which word rhymes with funny?
items.rationale: Sunny and funny both have the long e sound at the end, so they rhyme.

items.prompt: Which phrase from a poem helps you hear a sound?
items.rationale: “Rang loudly” describes a sound, so this phrase helps the reader hear the bell.

items.prompt: Which phrase from a story helps you see what something looks like?
items.rationale: A rainbow can be seen, so this phrase helps the reader picture the sky.

items.prompt: Which phrase from a story helps you feel how something feels when touched?
items.rationale: “Fur felt soft” tells how the puppy’s fur feels when it is touched.

items.prompt: Which phrase from a poem helps you taste something?
items.rationale: “Tasted salty” describes how the soup tastes to the person eating it.

items.prompt: How many vowel sounds are in the word picnic?
items.rationale: Picnic is read pic-nic, with one vowel sound in each part, for two vowel sounds total.

items.prompt: Which word has two vowel sounds?
items.rationale: Candle is read can-dle, with two vowel sounds: a and e.

items.prompt: Which vowel sound comes first in the word rabbit?
items.rationale: Rabbit is read rab-bit, so its first vowel sound is short a.

items.prompt: Which word is made of three vowel-sound parts?
items.rationale: Sunflower is read sun-flow-er, with one vowel sound in each of its three parts.

items.prompt: An information book says: “Sunflowers grow on tall stems. People eat the small seeds of a sunflower.” What is one new fact you learned?
choices: Sunflower seeds are food for people.
items.answer: Sunflower seeds are food for people.
items.rationale: The book says that people eat sunflower seeds, so this is a new fact the reader learned.

items.prompt: An information book says: “Camels live in dry places. A camel’s hump holds fat.” What is one new fact you learned about camels?
choices: Fat is stored in their humps.
Water is stored in their humps.
Food is stored in their humps.
Sand is stored in their humps.
items.answer: Fat is stored in their humps.
items.rationale: The book explains that a camel’s hump holds fat, not water, food, or sand.

items.prompt: An information book says: “Octopuses live in the ocean. Each octopus has eight arms.” Which statement is true in the text?
items.rationale: The text states that each octopus has eight arms.

items.prompt: An information book says: “Bees collect nectar from flowers. They use the nectar to make honey.” What could you tell someone about bees?
choices: They make honey from flower nectar.
They make honey from flower seeds.
They make honey from flower stems.
They make honey from flower leaves.
items.answer: They make honey from flower nectar.
items.rationale: The book says that bees collect nectar from flowers and use it to make honey.

items.prompt: An octopus has eight arms. Each arm has many small suckers that help it hold food and move underwater. Why does the author mention suckers?
choices: They help octopuses hold food and move.
They make ocean water taste salty.
They allow octopuses to breathe air.
They keep octopuses warm in deep water.
items.answer: They help octopuses hold food and move.
items.rationale: The author explains that suckers help an octopus hold food and move underwater.

items.prompt: Many desert animals stay active at night. The desert is very hot during the day, but it becomes cooler after sunset. What reason does the author give for this behavior?
choices: because daytime desert heat is too strong
because nighttime deserts have more plants
because all animals sleep during sunny days
because desert animals cannot see at night
items.answer: because daytime desert heat is too strong
items.rationale: The author gives the hot daytime desert as the reason many desert animals are active at night.

items.prompt: Penguins have thick feathers and a layer of fat. What reason supports the author's point that these coverings are useful?
choices: They help penguins stay warm in cold water.
They help penguins swim faster than fish.
They help penguins find and catch fish.
They help penguins store food for winter.
items.answer: They help penguins stay warm in cold water.
items.rationale: Thick feathers and fat are useful because they help penguins stay warm in cold water.

items.prompt: Plants need sunlight to grow. What reason does the author give to support this point?
choices: Plants use sunlight to make their food.
Roots use moonlight to help plants grow.
Wind carries sunlight into plant stems.
Animals share sunlight with nearby plants.
items.answer: Plants use sunlight to make their food.
items.rationale: The reason is that plants use sunlight to make the food they need to grow.

items.prompt: Read the story: At the park, Sam looked under a slide. He found his red cap. He put on the cap and smiled. Which detail tells what happened in the middle?
items.rationale: Finding the cap is the middle event between looking under the slide and putting on the cap.

items.prompt: Read the story: After the show, Max counted his puppets. He put them in a bag. He carried the bag to his car. Which detail tells what happened at the end?
choices: Max performed in the puppet show.
Max put the puppets in a bag.
Max bought a bag at the store.
Max carried the bag to his car.
items.answer: Max carried the bag to his car.
items.rationale: Carrying the bag to his car is the final event described in the story.

items.prompt: Read the story: Rain stopped falling. The sun came out. Kim and Lee went outside to play. Which detail happened just before Kim and Lee went outside?
choices: The rain stopped, and then the sun came out.
Kim found the gloves they would use outside.
Lee chose the game they would play outside.
The children came back inside after playing.
items.answer: The rain stopped, and then the sun came out.
items.rationale: The rain stopping and the sun coming out happen immediately before Kim and Lee went outside to play.

items.prompt: The text says, “Lin kicked the ball. It flew past the goalie and into the net.” A photo shows Lin in a soccer uniform beside the goal. What happened in the story?
choices: The goalie caught the flying ball.
The soccer game ended before kicking.
items.rationale: The words say the ball went into the net, while the photo identifies the activity as soccer.

items.prompt: An illustration shows a cat beside a full food bowl. The text says, “The hungry cat ran to its bowl when dinner was served.” What is the cat doing?
choices: The cat is going to eat its dinner.
The cat is hiding from its dinner.
The cat is filling an empty bowl.
The cat is running away from dinner.
items.answer: The cat is going to eat its dinner.
items.rationale: The picture shows food in the bowl, and the words explain that the hungry cat ran to it for dinner.

items.prompt: An illustration shows a tiny green plant growing from brown soil. The text says, “A farmer planted a seed. Rain and sunlight helped the seed become a plant.” What meaning do both give?
choices: A seed grew into a plant with water and light.
A farmer planted a green plant in the rain.
The farmer picked a plant from brown soil.
The seed stayed underground during sunlight.
items.answer: A seed grew into a plant with water and light.
items.rationale: The illustration shows a plant growing from soil, and the words explain that a seed received water and sunlight.

items.prompt: Read: “Rabbits have long ears that help them hear sounds. They eat plants and live for about 12 years. Large back legs help them hop from danger.” What is the paragraph mainly about?
choices: the homes rabbits build in fields
the life and body parts of rabbits
items.answer: the life and body parts of rabbits
items.rationale: The paragraph gives facts about a rabbit’s body, food, lifespan, and hopping.

items.prompt: Read: “Pandas are black and white. They eat bamboo and live in mountain forests in China. Pandas are usually gentle, but they can also bite.” Which detail is a fact the author gives?
choices: They live near the Indian Ocean.
They eat fish that swim in rivers.
They make their home in Chinese mountain forests.
They eat roots dug from desert soil.
items.answer: They make their home in Chinese mountain forests.
items.rationale: The author directly states that pandas live in mountain forests in China.

items.prompt: Read: “Arctic seals live in very cold water. Their thick fur and a layer of fat keep them warm. Their whiskers help them sense fish nearby.” Which fact explains how seals stay warm?
choices: Their whiskers help them find fish.
Their fur and body fat hold in heat.
Their large eyes let them see in dark water.
Their flippers make them swim faster.
items.answer: Their fur and body fat hold in heat.
items.rationale: The author explains that thick fur and a layer of fat help seals keep warm.

items.prompt: Read: “This bird has webbed feet, wings, and a heavy body. It cannot fly, but it uses its wings to swim and catches fish in cold water.” What is the main topic?
items.rationale: The facts describe a penguin, including its body, swimming, and fishing in cold oceans.

items.prompt: A nonfiction book says sea otters use rocks to break open shellfish. It also says mothers teach their pups which rocks work well. How are these two facts linked?
choices: The mother teaches the pup how to choose and use rocks.
The mother gives the pup extra shellfish to eat.
The pup finds a different food on the shore.
The rocks keep the mother safe from whales.
items.answer: The mother teaches the pup how to choose and use rocks.
items.rationale: Teaching the pup which rocks to use connects the fact about rocks with the fact about mothers teaching their pups.

items.prompt: Children plant bean seeds on Monday. It rains on Tuesday. The soil stays wet, and the seeds sprout on Friday. How are the rain and the sprouting connected?
choices: The wet soil helps the seeds grow and sprout.
The rain moves the seeds into new pots.
The children plant more seeds after Friday.
The soil becomes dry before the seeds sprout.
items.answer: The wet soil helps the seeds grow and sprout.
items.rationale: The rain keeps the soil wet, and the wet soil helps the planted seeds grow and sprout.

items.prompt: A beaver cuts branches from trees. It carries them to a stream and builds a dam. How are cutting the branches and building the dam connected?
choices: The branches are used to build the dam.
Cutting branches makes the dam hold back fish.
Building the dam gives the beaver more branches.
The stream carries branches to the beaver's home.
items.answer: The branches are used to build the dam.
items.rationale: The beaver cuts branches and then uses them to build a dam, so the first event provides materials for the second.

items.prompt: Desert animals rest in the shade to keep cool. Cactuses store water so they can grow in dry places. How are the two facts linked?
choices: Both help living things survive in hot, dry deserts.
Both show that desert animals drink from cactuses.
Both explain why the desert has no clouds.
Both show that all desert animals have long ears.
items.answer: Both help living things survive in hot, dry deserts.
items.rationale: Resting in shade and storing water are both ways that living things survive in hot, dry desert conditions.

items.prompt: Which part of a nonfiction book helps a reader quickly find the page where each section begins?
items.rationale: The contents page lists the book’s sections and the page where each section begins.

items.prompt: In a nonfiction book, “Types of Animals” appears above paragraphs about dogs, cats, and birds. What is “Types of Animals” called?
items.rationale: A heading names the topic of a section and helps readers quickly find information about that topic.

items.prompt: A reader sees an unfamiliar word in a book and wants to find its meaning. Which part of the book explains words used in the text?
items.rationale: A glossary gives the meanings of special or unfamiliar words used in a book.

items.prompt: It rains all morning. The street fills with shiny puddles. Two children put on boots and jump in the water. A dog shakes water over them. The children laugh and splash until the sun comes out. What happens for most of the story?
items.rationale: Most of the story describes the children laughing and jumping in the puddles.

items.prompt: Lina has an empty cardboard box. She cuts a door and a window, paints the box blue, and turns it upside down. She adds wheels and a string. The next day, she pulls her new toy across the room. Which title best matches what the story is mostly about?
choices: Pulling a Toy Across a Room
items.rationale: Lina’s main activity is transforming the box into a toy car, so the title reflects the main idea.

items.prompt: A boy walks home with his sister. They hear a bird chirping under a bench. They look, but cannot see it. A shop worker lets them lift the bench, and they find a small nest. The bird hops away safely, and the children smile. Which summary best tells what the story is mostly about?
choices: A bird sitting on a bench
A shop worker lifting a bench
items.rationale: The children work together to find and help the bird, which is the focus of the story.

items.prompt: A label on a box says “RETURN TO CLASS.” What should you do with the box?
items.rationale: The instruction “RETURN TO CLASS” tells the reader to take the box back to the classroom.

items.prompt: A sign on a door says “QUIET.” What should you do when you enter the room?
items.rationale: A sign reading “QUIET” asks people to make little noise when entering the room.

items.prompt: A cup has the words “MICROWAVE SAFE” printed on it. Can the cup go in a microwave?
items.rationale: The label says the cup is safe to use in a microwave.

items.prompt: Mia packed sandwiches and took her dog to the park. They ate under a tree and played fetch. What was the story mainly about?
choices: Mia and her dog enjoying a picnic together
Mia looking for a dog that had run away
Mia packing food for her classroom picnic
Mia visiting a pet store to buy a dog
items.answer: Mia and her dog enjoying a picnic together
items.rationale: The story centers on Mia sharing food and playing with her dog at the park.

items.prompt: Sam planted a seed in soil and watered it. On Friday, he saw a green leaf. Which choice tells the beginning and end?
choices: Sam planted a seed; later, a green leaf grew.
Sam found a leaf; later, he planted a seed.
Sam watered a plant; later, he made a pot.
Sam made soil; later, he gave away the plant.
items.answer: Sam planted a seed; later, a green leaf grew.
items.rationale: The story begins with Sam planting a seed and ends with a green leaf growing.

items.prompt: Lee flew his kite in the park. Wind pulled the string from his hand. The kite landed in a tree, and a worker brought it down. What happened last?
choices: A worker brought Lee's kite down.
The kite pulled the string from Lee's hand.
Lee took his kite to the park.
The worker climbed up and flew the kite.
items.answer: A worker brought Lee's kite down.
items.rationale: The final event was a worker bringing Lee's kite down from the tree.

items.prompt: Ben searched for his cap. His sister found it on the table. He put it on and went outside. Which choice best summarizes the story?
choices: Ben searched, and his sister found his cap.
Ben found his cap outside, then lost it again.
Ben's sister lost the cap, and Ben bought one.
Ben played outside before searching the house.
items.answer: Ben searched, and his sister found his cap.
items.rationale: This choice accurately includes the main event: Ben searched for his cap, and his sister found it.

items.prompt: A reader reaches the end of a sentence. What should the reader do?
items.rationale: A period marks the end of a sentence, so the reader should pause briefly before reading the next sentence.

items.prompt: Mia’s kitten was hiding under the bed. Mia said, “Come out, little kitty!” How should Mia read the quotation?
items.rationale: A soft, coaxing voice fits Mia’s gentle words to a hiding kitten.

items.prompt: Thunder cracked, and the frightened dog hid under the table. How should this text be read?
items.rationale: A tense, excited voice matches the sudden thunder and the frightened dog’s reaction.

items.prompt: Which choice shows the best way to read this text aloud? “The rain stopped. Sunlight lit the street. The children ran outside.”
choices: Pause at each period and use a lively voice.
Pause at each comma and use a sad voice.
Read quickly without pausing at periods.
Pause only at the end and use a flat voice.
items.answer: Pause at each period and use a lively voice.
items.rationale: The reader should pause at each period and use a lively voice to match the children happily running outside.

items.prompt: A rabbit hid carrots behind a fence. A fox said he could hide them better, led the rabbit away, and then ate the carrots. What lesson does this story teach?
choices: Be careful with people who trick you.
Keep food where everyone can see it.
items.answer: Be careful with people who trick you.
items.rationale: The fox tricks the rabbit, so the lesson is to be careful with people who cannot be trusted.

items.prompt: A hare laughed at a tortoise and challenged it to a race. The tortoise kept moving slowly and crossed the finish line first. What lesson does this story teach?
choices: Keep trying even when someone laughs.
The fastest animal always wins a race.
Never begin a race with a friend.
A race is better without other animals.
items.answer: Keep trying even when someone laughs.
items.rationale: The tortoise keeps trying and succeeds, teaching that steady effort matters even when others laugh.

items.prompt: A boy planted a seed but did not water it. The seed never grew. What simple lesson does the story teach?
choices: Things need care to grow properly.
Sunshine is the only thing plants need.
A seed can grow without any water.
Waiting is enough to make plants grow.
items.answer: Things need care to grow properly.
items.rationale: The seed did not grow because it was not cared for, showing that care is needed for growth.

items.prompt: A girl entered a cottage, ate the owner's porridge, broke a chair, and slept in a bed. The cottage owner returned and was angry. What lesson does the story teach?
choices: Treat other people's belongings with care.
A guest should stay for the whole day.
Food is safer outside a cottage.
Breaking furniture helps a guest rest.
items.answer: Treat other people's belongings with care.
items.rationale: The girl causes problems by using things without care, so the lesson is to respect other people's belongings.

items.prompt: Mina wears a red hat. Leo wears a red hat. What is one way to compare Mina and Leo?
choices: They are the same because both wear red hats.
They are different because both wear red hats.
Only Mina wears a red hat, not Leo.
Neither Mina nor Leo wears a red hat.
items.answer: They are the same because both wear red hats.
items.rationale: Both characters wear red hats, so they are alike in that way.

items.prompt: Lulu's story begins at school. Momo's story begins at school. Which comparison is true?
choices: The two stories have the same setting.
The two stories have different settings.
Only Lulu's story begins at school.
items.answer: The two stories have the same setting.
items.rationale: Both stories begin at school, so their settings are the same.

items.prompt: Pip washes a cup in one story. In another story, Pip waters a plant. What is one difference?
choices: Pip does different things in the two stories.
Pip does the same thing in both stories.
Both stories happen only at school.
Both stories end with a happy song.
items.answer: Pip does different things in the two stories.
items.rationale: Pip washes a cup in one story but waters a plant in the other.

items.prompt: Which event could happen only in a make-believe story?
choices: A child bakes bread with an adult.
A rabbit drives a bus to school.
A girl reads a book at home.
A dog runs across a grassy field.
items.answer: A rabbit drives a bus to school.
items.rationale: A rabbit driving a bus is make-believe because animals cannot do human activities. The other events could happen in real life.

items.prompt: In a story, a dog says, “I will wait by the gate.” What clue shows that the story is make-believe?
choices: The dog waits by a gate.
items.rationale: The dog speaking in words is the clearest clue because real dogs cannot talk. Having a dog or being outdoors could happen in real life.

items.prompt: Which beginning most likely belongs to a story that could really happen?
choices: A girl packed her lunch and walked to school.
A dragon carried the girl to school.
A bus grew wings and flew away.
A talking pencil gave her directions.
items.answer: A girl packed her lunch and walked to school.
items.rationale: A girl packing lunch and walking to school can happen in real life. Dragons, flying buses, and talking objects show make-believe.

items.prompt: Mia filled a bucket at the pond. Then the bucket became a small boat. What should a reader notice?
choices: The second event shows the story is make-believe.
The first event shows the story is make-believe.
Both events show the story is make-believe.
Neither event shows the story is make-believe.
items.answer: The second event shows the story is make-believe.
items.rationale: A bucket becoming a boat cannot really happen, so the second event gives a clue that the story is make-believe.
